new_statements.rule_in_words: The only prosodic statements found are second-hand surveys reporting that Resígaro is a two-tone language (high vs. low), a contrast attributed to Bora contact; no source opened says anything about word stress, its placement, or whether stress exists alongside tone. Allin 1976 (the primary grammar) is the only work likely to state the tone/stress facts first-hand and could not be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is described as a lexical/phonological property of words (data from Allin's wordlist, where high tone is marked with an acute accent); no domain (word vs phrase) or citation-form discussion. Seifart 2015 (p.105, Table 4) marks the tone claim as uncertain: 'phonological tone (?)' borrowed from Bora.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern data (Allin 1971-72 fieldwork; Seifart 2003-2009) come from the Andrade/Ocagane family at Puerto Isango on the Yaguasyacu/Ampiyacu, NE Peru, i.e. the Peruvian remnant variety; Rivet & de Wavrin's 1920s-30s wordlist is from the Caquetá (Colombia) and Aikhenvald 2001:184 suggests it may represent another, probably extinct, dialect. Glottolog has a single languoid resi1247; no separate code for the older Colombian variety.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Resígaro has two contrastive tones, high and low (minimal pairs). Stress is not an independent word-level category: it co-occurs with high tone as one (weak) phonetic aspect of the realisation of high tone, so prominence falls wherever the lexical/grammatical high tone falls; an extra 'pulse' is heard when a high tone follows a low tone.

Snippet q8/q17: level tones on short vowels, gliding tones on sequences of two unlike vowels and on long vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: Allin 1976 describes the Resígaro spoken by the last speakers at Puerto Isango / Brillo Nuevo on the Ampiyacu (Peru), the same variety Seifart 2011 and Aikhenvald 2001 draw on (their data come from Allin). No dialect distinction is at issue.

[...] Glides only occur on sequences of two vocoids, and are handled as sequences of high + low or low + high tone (cf. 1.3.3., below), and in consequence the system is one of register, not contour, tones." — p. 88, footnote 6 (to Rule 3b, low+high vowel sequences = two syllables): "This effect of a high tone on syllable boundaries may be explicable on phonetic and physiological grounds, in that high tone is generally produced more energetically than low tone. i.e., stress and high tone co-occur, the former being one of the aspects of the manifestation of the latter (though not a very pronounced aspect)." — p. 90: "The syllable is distributed in the phonological word. This is not analyzed in the present description".

new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and the existing Allin 1976 statement (which was stitched from Google Books snippets with the page unverified): the passage is verbatim on p. 88 as footnote 6 of vol. 1 (§2.2.3.3, Rule 3b), so the locator 'p. 88' is now verified against the book; adds the primary tone statement (§1.2.3 p. 72: two contrastive pitch levels, register system; §1.3.3 pp. 73-74: one tone per vowel) and the explicit statement that the phonological word is not analyzed (p. 90), i.e. no word-stress rule exists in the grammar. Agrees with Aikhenvald 2001 (two tones, no stress statement).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Resígaro has two contrastive register tones (high, low), one toneme per vowel (mora); glides are H+L / L+H over two vowels. There is no independent word-stress phoneme or placement rule: the only mention of stress (p. 88 fn. 6) says stress co-occurs with high tone as a weak phonetic concomitant of it, invoked to explain why a low+high vowel sequence is heard as two syllables. The phonological word (the 'stress-group' level of the tagmemic hierarchy) is explicitly left unanalyzed (p. 90), so the grammar gives no word-stress position.
new_statements.exceptions: none for stress; tone-related syllabification exceptions only (Rule 5 híí.?o 'this (horn)', fn. 8 híhuuu 'pigeon' onomatopoeic). Elsewhere (snippet q5, Part II) an imperative 'tone change' rule on the penultimate syllable of the verb is morphological tone, not stress (not in the scanned range).
new_statements.identity_note: Resígaro as spoken by Allin's principal informant(s) in the Bora-Ocaina area of the Peruvian Putumayo/Ampiyacu (fieldwork 1971-74, SIL Peru); the thesis treats a single variety, no dialects distinguished.

tone.quote: El resígaro es una lengua aglutinante y tonal. En cuanto su inventario fonológico, esta lengua presenta un amplio número de consonantes que asciende a treinta y posee diez vocales entre cortas y largas.
